props.title: The Life of Jesus

sections.content: Bruno Dumont's The Life of Jesus (1997) marks a stark departure from traditional religious cinema, offering an unflinching look at rural French youth through a secular lens. Unlike reverential biopics like The Greatest Story Ever Told (1965) or Jesus of Nazareth (1977), Dumont's film follows Freddy, an epileptic teenager in a depressed northern French town whose name ironically references Jesus but whose life embodies modern spiritual emptiness. The film's raw naturalism and use of non-professional actors established Dumont's signature style that would influence later works like Humanité (1999) and Twentynine Palms (2003).

sections.content: Dumont's approach connects to a broader European tradition of depicting spiritual crisis through secular stories, exemplified by Robert Bresson's Mouchette (1967) and L'Argent (1983). The Life of Jesus's brutal honesty about sexuality, violence, and racism among disenfranchised youth creates an anti-hagiography that questions moral foundations in modern society. This technique influenced later French films like La Haine (1995) and Fat Girl (2001). SUBHEAD: The New French Extremity Movement

The Life of Jesus helped pave the way for the New French Extremity movement, which includes works like Irreversible (2002) and Trouble Every Day (2001). These films share a commitment to shocking authenticity and exploration of body horror as metaphor for social decay. Dumont's unflinching camera and focus on physical experiences - from epileptic seizures to sexual encounters - established a visual language that later directors would build upon.
